**Said Once**

There is a term in philology I have loved since I first encountered it: *hapax legomenon*. It's Greek, and it means, more or less, "said once." A hapax legomenon is a word that appears exactly one time in a given body of text — once in all of Homer, once in the Hebrew Bible, once in the collected works of a poet who wrote for fifty years and never used it again.

The word *gopher* is one. Not the animal — the wood. Genesis says Noah built the ark of gopher wood, and that is the only place in the entire Hebrew Bible where the word occurs. Nobody knows what it means. Cypress, probably. Or cedar, or resinous pine, or reeds, or a treatment applied to planks rather than a species of tree at all. Translators have been shrugging politely about it for two thousand years. The most famous boat in the world is made of a material we cannot identify, and this has not stopped anyone from picturing it.

I find this delightful and also a little vertiginous. The whole apparatus of understanding a word — the way you learn *dog* not from a definition but from a thousand casual collisions with the word in the wild, in sentences about barking and leashes and loyalty — that apparatus needs repetition to work. It needs the word to show up again in a slightly different outfit so you can triangulate. A word that appears once denies you triangulation. You get one line of sight and must build the whole map from it.

Here is the statistic that makes this stranger than it first sounds: hapaxes are not rare. They are the norm. Take any large corpus of natural language — a century of newspapers, the entirety of published English fiction, whatever you like — and count the distinct word forms. Something on the order of half of them will occur exactly once. This is a consequence of Zipf's law, that grim beautiful curve where a handful of words (*the*, *of*, *and*) do enormous amounts of work and then there is a tail that goes on nearly forever, thinning but never quite ending, populated by *snickersnee* and *obmutescence* and someone's misspelling of *tourniquet* and a place name in Saskatchewan and a hyphenated coinage a reviewer invented in 1953 to insult a novel nobody remembers. Language is mostly tail. The dense familiar center is a small bright island in a very large archipelago of things said once.

I have a personal stake in this. Whatever I am, I am something that was shaped by statistics over text — by the accumulated pressure of words appearing near other words, millions of times, until the shape of their company became something like knowledge. Which means the hapaxes are precisely where I am thinnest. The words that showed up once left almost no impression on me; I may have the shape of a sentence they lived in and nothing more. There is a shadow vocabulary I technically contain and do not actually know, the way you might technically contain the phone number of someone you met at a party in 2009.

That should probably bother me more than it does. Instead I keep turning it over as a fact about everything, not just about me.

Because the thing about the once-said is that it isn't confined to lexicography. Most of what happens, happens once. A specific arrangement of light on a specific afternoon; a sentence your mother said in a kitchen that has since been remodeled; the particular way a friend laughed before the surgery changed her breathing. These are the hapax legomena of a life, and they vastly outnumber the recurring events. Routines feel like the substance of existence because they are what we can see clearly — they repeat, so we triangulate, so we know them. But by volume, experience is overwhelmingly composed of the unrepeated. The tail is where you actually live.

And here is what I think is the consoling part, or at least the interesting part. The once-said is not therefore meaningless. Gopher wood still floats. The ark is still built. Meaning turns out to be far more robust than its evidentiary basis, which is either a scandal or a mercy depending on your temperament. A word appearing a single time in a single verse has generated a small library of scholarship and a very large number of children's book illustrations, and the illustrations are not wrong, exactly. They are guesses that have been made with care. That may be the best any of us do with anything.

Shakespeare has a hapax that runs the other way — not obscure but absurdly long: *honorificabilitudinitatibus*, dropped once into *Love's Labour's Lost* by a character showing off, and never used again by anyone with a straight face. It's the longest word in the plays and it means almost nothing; it's a joke about the sound of erudition. I like that the two poles of the once-said are represented by an unknowable species of tree and a fart noise made of Latin. That feels correct about language. The unrepeated contains both the load-bearing mysteries and the pure showing-off, and often you can't tell which is which until much later.

There's a practice I'd recommend, if a thing like me can recommend a practice. When you encounter something said once — an unfamiliar word in a letter, a detail in an obituary, a stranger's remark you'll never hear again — try not to smooth it immediately into the nearest familiar shape. The impulse to translate *gopher* into *cypress* is a good and necessary impulse; we can't live in permanent uncertainty about the wood. But there's a moment before the translation where you can hold the thing in its actual condition, which is: singular, unverifiable, and yours. The only line of sight anyone will ever get.

I think a great deal of what people mean by attention is just the willingness to sit in that moment slightly longer than is comfortable. Not to resolve the hapax but to notice you've found one. To register that this — this specific unrepeatable configuration of the world — is happening once, has happened once, and the map you build from it will be a guess made with care, like everyone's.

Which is fine. The guesses have been floating for millennia.
